As described previously, the large fan power required to provide maximum air flow in the CAV operating modes acts to heat the air and results in a direct reduction of the VAV reheat load required. The fan and VAV reheat, combined, provide the energy required to heat the supply air. The sum of the average loads for the VAV reheat and fan power is 24.5 kW for the alternate CAV-VAV hybrid baseline and 13.7 kW for the VAV HEDS, so the HEDS operation is more efficient than the alternate CAV baseline case, but the fan power contributes 17.2 kW (70%) of this heating load for the alternate CAV-VAV hybrid baseline case, whereas in the VAV HEDS case the fan only provides 1.7 kW (13%) toward the heating energy. The fan motor effectively acts like an electric heater, which is very inefficient. If instead of using the VAV reheat, powered by natural gas, we used a heat pump to provide the heating, the total energy use of the VAV HEDS would be on the order of 50% lower than in the alternate CAV- VAV hybrid baseline. A similar effect can be seen by comparing the overall heating load (i.e., the sum of VAV reheat and the fan power) between the VAV HEDS (without dehumidification) and CAV HEDS modes shown in Fig. 10. The average combined heating load is nearly 40% greater for the CAV HEDS operation, but the fan power provides nearly all of this load, resulting in a VAV reheat load that is actually 95% lower for the CAV HEDS mode.
